key_terms.meaning: N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>c</sub>(C<sub>A,b</sub> − C<sub>A,s</sub>); mol/(m²·s), with bulk and surface concentrations C<sub>A,b</sub> and C<sub>A,s</sub>.
Flux per unit concentration driving force; N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>c</sub> ΔC<sub>A</sub>; units m/s.
Gas-side coefficient; N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>G</sub>(p<sub>A</sub> − p<sub>A,i</sub>); usually mol/(m²·s·Pa).
Liquid-side coefficient; N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>x</sub>(x<sub>i</sub> − x<sub>A</sub>); kmol/(m²·s) per unit mole-fraction difference.
1/K<sub>y</sub> = 1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub> for dilute equilibrium y* = m x; based on gas mole fraction.
1/K<sub>x</sub> = 1/k<sub>x</sub> + 1/(m k<sub>y</sub>); based on liquid mole fraction.
Sh = k<sub>c</sub> L/D<sub>AB</sub>; dimensionless mass transfer coefficient with length L and diffusivity D<sub>AB</sub>.
Sc = μ/(ρD<sub>AB</sub>) = ν/D<sub>AB</sub>; momentum diffusivity divided by mass diffusivity.
Model with a stagnant film of thickness δ; k<sub>c</sub> = D<sub>AB</sub>/δ.
Eddies expose fresh surface for time t; k<sub>c</sub> = 2√(D<sub>AB</sub>/(πt)).
Surface elements renew at rate s; k<sub>c</sub> = √(D<sub>AB</sub> s).
Turbulent mixing contribution to mass flux; total flux uses D<sub>AB</sub> + ε<sub>M</sub>; units m²/s.
j<sub>D</sub> = (k<sub>c</sub>/u)Sc<sup>2/3</sup> = f/2; links mass transfer to friction factor f.
Two stagnant films in series with equilibrium at the interface; resistances add.
A stage whose leaving vapour and liquid are in equilibrium; stage efficiency converts ideal stages into real trays.
E<sub>MV</sub> = (y<sub>n</sub> − y<sub>n+1</sub>)/(y<sub>n</sub>* − y<sub>n+1</sub>); the actual vapour change on a tray over the change to equilibrium with the liquid leaving it.

key_terms.term: Height of a transfer unit H<sub>OG</sub>
key_terms.meaning: H<sub>OG</sub> = G/(K<sub>y</sub> a); packed height per transfer unit; G is molar gas flux.
N<sub>OG</sub> = ∫ dy/(y − y*) from the outlet to the inlet gas composition; (y<sub>1</sub> − y<sub>2</sub>)/(y − y*)<sub>lm</sub> for straight lines.
E = flux with reaction / flux without reaction; raises liquid-side mass transfer.
Ha = √(k D<sub>AB</sub>)/k<sub>L</sub> for first-order reaction; k is reaction rate constant.

takeaways: A convective mass transfer coefficient k<sub>c</sub> turns a complex flow problem into a simple flux equation N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>c</sub> ΔC<sub>A</sub>.
Individual film coefficients add as resistances; the overall coefficient depends on which phase's driving force you choose.
Dimensionless correlations write Sh as a function of Re, Sc and geometry, so one measured system predicts another.
Film theory makes k<sub>c</sub> proportional to D; penetration and surface-renewal theories make it proportional to √D, which matches data at gas–liquid surfaces.
Momentum, heat and mass analogies let a friction factor or heat transfer coefficient estimate k<sub>c</sub>.
At the interface the two phases are in equilibrium, so y<sub>i</sub> = m x<sub>i</sub>, and the two film resistances set the flux.
An ideal stage is an equilibrium stage; stage efficiency converts ideal stages into real trays.
Tray columns are counted in ideal stages divided by an overall efficiency; packed columns are sized by Z = H<sub>OG</sub> × N<sub>OG</sub>.
A reaction in the liquid film can raise flux by E, and Ha tells whether the reaction is slow or fast.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine a coefficient definition, the resistances-in-series derivation, one correlation or theory, and a staged or packed contactor calculation. Each model answer below works its numbers through to the result.

bank.q: Define the convective mass transfer coefficient k<sub>c</sub> for transfer between a solid surface and a flowing fluid. Write the flux equation, state the unit of every term, and give the equivalent gas-phase forms. Illustrate with a benzoic acid plate (solubility 3.44 kg/m³ in water, M = 122.1 kg/kmol) dissolving into water with k<sub>c</sub> = 2.0×10⁻⁵ m/s.
outline: Definition: flux per unit concentration difference
Why k<sub>c</sub> replaces an unknown film thickness
Gas forms k<sub>G</sub> and k<sub>y</sub> and their conversion
Worked number for the benzoic acid plate
answer: When a fluid flows past a surface that gives up or takes up species A, the flux depends on the flow, the geometry and the fluid properties, and no film thickness can be measured. The convective mass transfer coefficient k<sub>c</sub> lumps all of that into one number, defined as the molar flux per unit concentration difference between the surface and the bulk fluid.

answer.text: The defining equation and its units:
answer.pre:
N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>c</sub> (C<sub>Ai</sub> − C<sub>A</sub>∞)

N<sub>A</sub>    molar flux of A, mol/(m²·s)
C<sub>Ai</sub>   concentration of A in the fluid at the surface, mol/m³
C<sub>A</sub>∞   concentration of A in the well-mixed bulk, mol/m³
k<sub>c</sub>    mass transfer coefficient, m/s

answer: The unit of k<sub>c</sub> follows from the equation: mol/(m²·s) divided by mol/m³ is m/s. It looks like a velocity but it is not the fluid speed; it measures how fast the near-wall layer is renewed and thinned by the flow. For a stagnant film of thickness δ, molecular diffusion gives k<sub>c</sub> = D<sub>AB</sub>/δ, so a moving fluid behaves like a film of thickness D<sub>AB</sub>/k<sub>c</sub>.

A local coefficient applies at one point of the surface; an average coefficient applies to the whole area, so that total transfer rate = k<sub>c,avg</sub> × area × driving force. Design uses averages.

answer.text: For a gas the driving force can be written three ways, and each has its own coefficient:

answer: The coefficient also depends on what the other species does. For A through stagnant B the flux is larger than for equimolar counter-diffusion at the same driving force, and the two types are linked by k<sub>G</sub> p<sub>Bm</sub> = k′<sub>G</sub> P. For a dilute solute p<sub>Bm</sub> ≈ P and the difference vanishes.
Benzoic acid example. The water at the plate surface is saturated: C<sub>Ai</sub> = 3.44/122.1 = 0.0282 kmol/m³ = 28.2 mol/m³. Fresh water flows past, so C<sub>A</sub>∞ ≈ 0.
Flux: N<sub>A</sub> = 2.0×10⁻⁵ × (28.2 − 0) = 5.63×10⁻⁴ mol/(m²·s). Unit check: (m/s)(mol/m³) = mol/(m²·s).

For a plate of 0.10 m²: rate = 5.63×10⁻⁴ × 0.10 = 5.63×10⁻⁵ mol/s = 5.63×10⁻⁵ × 122.1 × 3600 = 24.8 g of acid per hour. Weighing the plate before and after a timed run is exactly how such coefficients are measured.

Check: k<sub>c</sub> = 2.0×10⁻⁵ m/s corresponds to an equivalent film of D<sub>AB</sub>/k<sub>c</sub> = 1.0×10⁻⁹/2.0×10⁻⁵ = 50 µm for a liquid diffusivity of 1.0×10⁻⁹ m²/s, a sensible thickness for a slow liquid flow.

bank.q: Derive the relation between individual and overall gas-phase mass transfer coefficients for dilute absorption, 1/K<sub>y</sub> = 1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub>, and the matching relation for K<sub>x</sub>. Define m, state the assumptions, and apply the result to k<sub>y</sub> = 0.025 kmol/(m²·s), k<sub>x</sub> = 0.20 kmol/(m²·s) and m = 0.8.
outline: Film fluxes N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>y</sub>(y − y<sub>i</sub>) = k<sub>x</sub>(x<sub>i</sub> − x)
Interface equilibrium y<sub>i</sub> = m x<sub>i</sub>; define y* and x*
Add the drops on the gas basis
Same on the liquid basis; K<sub>x</sub> = m K<sub>y</sub>
answer: Consider a solute crossing from bulk gas (mole fraction y) to bulk liquid (mole fraction x). At steady state the same flux N<sub>A</sub> passes through the gas film and the liquid film, and no solute collects at the interface:

The interface itself offers no resistance, so the compositions there are in equilibrium. For a dilute solution the equilibrium line is straight, y* = m x, where m is its slope (dimensionless on a mole-fraction plot). So y<sub>i</sub> = m x<sub>i</sub>.

Interface compositions cannot be sampled, so define overall driving forces from bulk values: y* = m x is the gas composition in equilibrium with the bulk liquid, and x* = y/m the liquid composition in equilibrium with the bulk gas. Then N<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>y</sub>(y − y*) = K<sub>x</sub>(x* − x) defines the overall coefficients.

answer.text: Gas basis: split the overall drop at the interface and write each part from its film equation.
answer.pre:
y − y* = (y − y<sub>i</sub>) + (y<sub>i</sub> − y*)
      = N<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>y</sub> + m(x<sub>i</sub> − x)
      = N<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>y</sub> + m N<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>x</sub>
N<sub>A</sub>/K<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>A</sub> (1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub>)

1/K<sub>y</sub> = 1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub>

answer.text: Liquid basis: the same steps with x.
answer.pre:
x* − x = (x* − x<sub>i</sub>) + (x<sub>i</sub> − x)
      = (y − y<sub>i</sub>)/m + (x<sub>i</sub> − x)
      = N<sub>A</sub>/(m k<sub>y</sub>) + N<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>x</sub>

1/K<sub>x</sub> = 1/(m k<sub>y</sub>) + 1/k<sub>x</sub>

answer: Comparing the two sums, 1/K<sub>x</sub> = (1/m)(1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub>) = 1/(m K<sub>y</sub>), so K<sub>x</sub> = m K<sub>y</sub>. The factor m converts a liquid-side composition difference into the equivalent gas-side one; without it a Δx resistance would be added to a Δy resistance.

Assumptions: steady state; equilibrium at the interface; a straight equilibrium line over the range from x to x<sub>i</sub> (for a curved line m becomes the chord slope m′ in K<sub>y</sub> and m″ in K<sub>x</sub>); dilute solute so the coefficients do not change with concentration; the same interfacial area for both films.

answer.text: Applying the result:

answer: With 91 % of the resistance in the gas film this system is gas-film controlled, as for a very soluble gas such as ammonia in water: a small m makes the liquid term small. Raising gas turbulence would pay; stirring the liquid harder would barely change K<sub>y</sub>.
Check: from 1/K<sub>x</sub> = 1/(m k<sub>y</sub>) + 1/k<sub>x</sub> = 1/(0.8 × 0.025) + 1/0.20 = 50 + 5 = 55, K<sub>x</sub> = 0.0182 kmol/(m²·s), the same as m K<sub>y</sub>.

bank.q: Compare the film, penetration and surface-renewal theories of mass transfer. Give the k<sub>L</sub> expression from each, state one limitation of each, and evaluate all three for CO₂ (D = 1.9×10⁻⁹ m²/s) absorbed into a liquid surface that is renewed every 0.5 s on average.
answer: All three theories try to explain the liquid-film coefficient k<sub>L</sub> in N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>L</sub>(C<sub>Ai</sub> − C<sub>A</sub>) from a simple picture of the liquid next to the interface. Each needs one parameter that must be fitted to a measurement, so none predicts k<sub>L</sub> from first principles.

Film theory (Whitman). A stagnant layer of thickness δ sits at the interface; beyond it the liquid is well mixed. Steady diffusion across the layer gives a straight profile and k<sub>L</sub> = D/δ. The parameter δ is chosen to match the measured k<sub>L</sub>. Limitation: it predicts k<sub>L</sub> ∝ D, while measured coefficients at gas–liquid surfaces usually vary as D<sup>0.5</sup> to D<sup>0.7</sup>; and no real stagnant layer of that thickness exists.

Penetration theory (Higbie). An eddy carries a fresh liquid element to the surface, where it stays for a fixed exposure time t. During that time the solute diffuses into it as into a semi-infinite medium, because the penetration depth √(D t) is small. Averaging the unsteady flux over t gives k<sub>L</sub> = 2√(D/(πt)). Limitation: every element is given the same age, which is reasonable for a falling film or a rising bubble but not for a stirred, turbulent surface.

Surface-renewal theory (Danckwerts). Elements are replaced at random, with a fractional renewal rate s (s⁻¹) independent of their age; averaging over the resulting age distribution gives k<sub>L</sub> = √(D s). Limitation: s cannot be measured directly and must be fitted, so the theory gives the √D dependence but not the magnitude.

answer.text: For CO₂ with t = 0.5 s (and s = 1/t would be a rough first guess):

head: Theory
Formula
Working
k<sub>L</sub>, m/s
rows: film, δ fitted to the penetration value

answer: To make surface renewal match penetration exactly, s = k<sub>L</sub>²/D = (6.96×10⁻⁵)²/1.9×10⁻⁹ = 2.55 s⁻¹, not 2.0: the factor 4/π between the two models (s = 4/(π t)) comes from the different age distributions. Either way k<sub>L</sub> is of order 10⁻⁴ m/s, the usual size for liquid films in packed towers.
Dependence on contact time: halving t to 0.25 s raises the penetration k<sub>L</sub> by √2 to 9.84×10⁻⁵ m/s, which is why short packing elements and frequent surface renewal improve absorption.

answer.text: Comparison:

answer: Conclusion: the theories agree on magnitude only after fitting, and differ in how k<sub>L</sub> scales with D. A second solute with a different D, measured in the same equipment, tells them apart. Film theory stays the working tool for two-resistance and reaction calculations because its algebra is simplest and its enhancement factors are close to those of the other two.

bank.q: Explain the two-resistance theory of interphase mass transfer. Why may the interface be assumed to be at equilibrium? Support the argument with an estimate for oxygen (partial pressure 0.21 atm at 298 K) absorbing into water with k<sub>L</sub> = 4.0×10⁻⁵ m/s and saturation concentration 0.26 mol/m³.
outline: Two films in series with the interface between
Kinetic-theory estimate of the interface exchange rate
Interface point on the y–x diagram
answer: Whitman's two-resistance theory pictures the region near a gas–liquid interface as two films in series: a gas film, across which the solute mole fraction falls from the bulk value y to y<sub>i</sub>, and a liquid film, across which it falls from x<sub>i</sub> to the bulk value x. Beyond the films each phase is well mixed.

At steady state nothing accumulates at the interface, so the same flux crosses both films: N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>y</sub>(y − y<sub>i</sub>) = k<sub>x</sub>(x<sub>i</sub> − x). The bulk phases are not in equilibrium; that difference is what drives the transfer.

The third assumption is that the interface itself has no resistance, so y<sub>i</sub> and x<sub>i</sub> lie on the equilibrium curve, y<sub>i</sub> = m x<sub>i</sub> for a straight line. This closes the problem: three equations fix y<sub>i</sub>, x<sub>i</sub> and N<sub>A</sub>.
Why equilibrium is reasonable: molecules strike the interface from the gas far faster than the films can carry them. Kinetic theory gives the striking rate as p/√(2π M R T).

The film-limited flux into water is at most N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>L</sub> C<sub>sat</sub> = 4.0×10⁻⁵ × 0.26 = 1.04×10⁻⁵ mol/(m²·s). The interface exchange capacity is about 953/1.04×10⁻⁵ ≈ 9×10⁷ times larger. Even if only a small fraction of the collisions led to dissolution, the departure from equilibrium needed to pass the film flux would be a negligible fraction of the total driving force. The interface only fails to be at equilibrium when a surfactant layer or a very high flux slows the crossing itself.

On a y–x diagram the bulk point (x, y) lies above the equilibrium line for absorption. A line of slope −k<sub>x</sub>/k<sub>y</sub> drawn from it meets the equilibrium line at the interface point (x<sub>i</sub>, y<sub>i</sub>); the vertical distance y − y<sub>i</sub> is the gas-film drop and the horizontal distance x<sub>i</sub> − x the liquid-film drop.

Because the drops are in series, resistances add: 1/K<sub>y</sub> = 1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub>. The film with the larger share controls: the gas film for very soluble gases (small m), the liquid film for sparingly soluble gases such as the oxygen here, where nearly all the resistance is on the liquid side.

Check: for oxygen m is about 4×10⁴ (Henry's constant in atmospheres at 1 atm total pressure), so m/k<sub>x</sub> dwarfs 1/k<sub>y</sub> for any realistic coefficients, and the whole flux estimate rests on k<sub>L</sub> alone, as used above.

bank.q: A dilute solute is absorbed with k<sub>y</sub> = 0.030 kmol/(m²·s), k<sub>x</sub> = 0.050 kmol/(m²·s) and equilibrium y* = 3.0x. At one point in the column y = 0.060 and x = 0.005. Calculate K<sub>y</sub> and K<sub>x</sub>, the percentage of the resistance in the gas film, the flux and the interface compositions.
outline: 1/K<sub>y</sub> and 1/K<sub>x</sub> with m in the right place
Which film controls and what to do
answer: Data: k<sub>y</sub> = 0.030 and k<sub>x</sub> = 0.050 kmol/(m²·s) per unit mole-fraction difference, m = 3.0, bulk y = 0.060 and x = 0.005.

answer.text: Resistances on the gas basis:

answer: Shares: gas film 33.3/93.3 = 35.7 %, liquid film 60.0/93.3 = 64.3 %. The shares are the same on either basis (11.1/31.1 = 35.7 %).
Overall driving force: y* = m x = 3.0 × 0.005 = 0.015, so N<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>y</sub>(y − y*) = 0.0107 × (0.060 − 0.015) = 4.82×10⁻⁴ kmol/(m²·s).

answer.text: Check the flux three ways:

answer: Interpretation: neither film passes the usual 80 % mark, but the liquid film carries almost two-thirds. Doubling k<sub>x</sub> would cut 1/K<sub>y</sub> to 33.3 + 30.0 = 63.3 and raise K<sub>y</sub> by 47 %; doubling k<sub>y</sub> would give 16.7 + 60.0 = 76.7, a 22 % gain. Effort on the liquid side (better wetting, more liquid turbulence, or a reacting solvent) pays more.

Effect of the solvent: a solvent in which the solute is three times more soluble (m = 1.0) gives 1/K<sub>y</sub> = 33.3 + 20.0 = 53.3 and K<sub>y</sub> = 0.0188 kmol/(m²·s); with y* = 0.005 the flux becomes 0.0188 × (0.060 − 0.005) = 1.03×10⁻³ kmol/(m²·s), more than twice as large, and the gas film now carries 62.5 % of the resistance. Solubility moves the controlling film as strongly as any change in flow.

bank.q: Air at 300 K and 1 atm with 30 % relative humidity flows at 3.0 m/s along a pan of water 0.60 m long (in the flow direction) and 0.40 m wide, kept at 300 K. Take ν = 1.57×10⁻⁵ m²/s and D<sub>AB</sub> = 2.6×10⁻⁵ m²/s for water vapour in air, and a vapour pressure of 3.54 kPa. Estimate k<sub>c</sub> and the evaporation rate. State all assumptions.
outline: Sc and the laminar flat-plate correlation
Driving force from vapour pressure and humidity
answer: Geometry: the pan surface acts as a flat plate with L = 0.60 m in the flow direction and area 0.60 × 0.40 = 0.24 m².
Regime: Re = uL/ν = 3.0 × 0.60/1.57×10⁻⁵ = 1.15×10⁵, below about 5×10⁵, so the boundary layer stays laminar over the whole pan.
Schmidt number: Sc = ν/D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.57×10⁻⁵/2.6×10⁻⁵ = 0.604, Sc<sup>1/3</sup> = 0.845.

answer.text: Average Sherwood number from the laminar flat-plate correlation:

answer: Coefficient: k<sub>c</sub> = Sh D<sub>AB</sub>/L = 190.0 × 2.6×10⁻⁵/0.60 = 8.23×10⁻³ m/s. The local value at the trailing edge is half the average for a laminar plate, 4.1×10⁻³ m/s.
Driving force: the air at the water surface is saturated, C<sub>Ai</sub> = 3540/(8.314 × 300) = 1.42 mol/m³; the bulk air holds 30 % of that, 0.425 mol/m³; ΔC = 0.70 × 1.42 = 0.994 mol/m³.
Flux: N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>c</sub> ΔC = 8.23×10⁻³ × 0.994 = 8.18×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s).

answer.text: Effect of air speed (laminar throughout, Sh ∝ Re<sup>1/2</sup>):

answer: Assumptions: (1) the water surface is held at 300 K, as stated; an unheated pan would cool towards the wet-bulb temperature and evaporate less. (2) Properties are evaluated at the film temperature, here 300 K since surface and air are equal. (3) The pan edge is flush and the flow undisturbed, so the boundary layer starts at the leading edge of the water. (4) Low flux: water vapour is dilute (y<sub>A</sub> ≤ 0.035), so the stagnant-air correction P/p<sub>Bm</sub> ≈ 1.02 is neglected. (5) The plate is smooth and the free stream is not turbulent.

Check with the Chilton–Colburn analogy: the laminar average skin-friction coefficient is 1.328/√Re = 1.328/338.6 = 3.92×10⁻³, so j<sub>D</sub> = 1.96×10⁻³ and Sh = j<sub>D</sub> Re Sc<sup>1/3</sup> = 1.96×10⁻³ × 1.15×10⁵ × 0.845 = 190, the same value, because the laminar correlation and the analogy rest on the same boundary-layer solution.
Check on size: the equivalent film thickness D<sub>AB</sub>/k<sub>c</sub> = 2.6×10⁻⁵/8.23×10⁻³ = 3.2 mm, a reasonable boundary-layer scale for 3 m/s air over 0.6 m.

bank.q: A tray absorber treats gas with y<sub>N+1</sub> = 0.020 (solute mole fraction, dilute) to give y<sub>1</sub> = 0.0020, using solute-free liquid at L/G = 1.5. The equilibrium line is y* = 1.0x and every tray has a Murphree vapour efficiency E<sub>MV</sub> = 0.60. Find the number of ideal stages, then the number of real trays both by a tray-by-tray calculation and by the overall efficiency.
outline: Murphree relation on each real tray
Overall efficiency from Lewis and comparison
Round up and check the outlet
answer: Number the trays from the top. Gas leaves tray 1 at y<sub>1</sub> = 0.0020; liquid enters at x<sub>0</sub> = 0. A solute balance from the top to below tray n gives the operating line y<sub>n+1</sub> = y<sub>1</sub> + (L/G)(x<sub>n</sub> − x<sub>0</sub>) = 0.0020 + 1.5 x<sub>n</sub>.

Ideal stages: A = L/(mG) = 1.5/1.0 = 1.5. Kremser: N = ln[((y<sub>N+1</sub> − m x<sub>0</sub>)/(y<sub>1</sub> − m x<sub>0</sub>))(1 − 1/A) + 1/A]/ln A = ln[10 × 0.333 + 0.667]/ln 1.5 = ln 4.00/0.405 = 3.42 ideal stages.

answer.text: Real trays. On tray n the leaving vapour satisfies the Murphree definition, with y<sub>n</sub>* = m x<sub>n</sub> for the liquid leaving the same tray:
answer.pre:
y<sub>n</sub> = y<sub>n+1</sub> + E<sub>MV</sub> (m x<sub>n</sub> − y<sub>n+1</sub>)
y<sub>n+1</sub> = 0.0020 + 1.5 x<sub>n</sub>
=> x<sub>n</sub> = [y<sub>n</sub> − 0.4 × 0.0020] / (0.4 × 1.5 + 0.6 × 1.0)
       = (y<sub>n</sub> − 0.0008)/1.2

answer.text: Start at the top with y<sub>1</sub> = 0.0020 and work down:

answer: Check tray 1: E<sub>MV</sub> = (y<sub>1</sub> − y<sub>2</sub>)/(y<sub>1</sub>* − y<sub>2</sub>) = (0.0020 − 0.0035)/(0.0010 − 0.0035) = 0.60. Six trays bring the entering gas only to 0.01889; the seventh passes 0.020. By interpolation the duty needs 6 + (0.020 − 0.01889)/(0.02461 − 0.01889) = 6.2 trays, so 7 real trays are installed.

Overall efficiency: with straight lines and a constant E<sub>MV</sub>, Lewis's relation applies with λ = mG/L = 1/1.5 = 0.667: E<sub>o</sub> = ln[1 + 0.60 × (0.667 − 1)]/ln 0.667 = ln 0.800/ln 0.667 = 0.223/0.405 = 0.550.
Real trays = 3.42/0.550 = 6.2, rounded up to 7, matching the tray-by-tray result.

Note that E<sub>o</sub> = 0.55 is below E<sub>MV</sub> = 0.60, because λ < 1 in an absorber. Dividing the ideal count by E<sub>MV</sub> instead (3.42/0.60 = 5.7, so 6 trays) would leave the outlet at 0.0035 instead of 0.0020, missing the specification.

Check: the overall balance gives the bottom liquid x<sub>N</sub> = (0.020 − 0.0020)/1.5 = 0.0120 for the exact duty. Only 0.2 of the seventh tray is needed, so with seven trays the outlet gas falls a little below 0.0020 and the specification is met with a small margin.

bank.q: A packed absorber removes 95 % of a solute from gas with y<sub>1</sub> = 0.030 using solute-free liquid at 1.4 times the minimum liquid rate. The equilibrium line is y* = 1.1x, G = 0.015 kmol/(m²·s) and K<sub>y</sub> a = 0.040 kmol/(m³·s). Calculate H<sub>OG</sub>, N<sub>OG</sub> and the packed height Z.
outline: End driving forces and log mean
N<sub>OG</sub> by log mean and by the absorption-factor formula
answer: Outlet gas: 95 % removal gives y<sub>2</sub> = 0.05 × 0.030 = 0.0015. Liquid enters solute-free, x<sub>2</sub> = 0. Subscript 1 is the bottom, 2 the top.

Minimum liquid rate: the liquid leaving can at best reach equilibrium with the entering gas, x<sub>1,max</sub> = y<sub>1</sub>/m = 0.030/1.1 = 0.0273. So (L/G)_min = (y<sub>1</sub> − y<sub>2</sub>)/(x<sub>1,max</sub> − x<sub>2</sub>) = 0.0285/0.0273 = 1.045.

answer.text: End driving forces:

answer: Cross-check with the absorption-factor form: A = (L/G)/m = 1.463/1.1 = 1.33; N<sub>OG</sub> = ln[(1 − 1/A)(y<sub>1</sub> − m x<sub>2</sub>)/(y<sub>2</sub> − m x<sub>2</sub>) + 1/A]/(1 − 1/A) = ln[0.248 × 20 + 0.752]/0.248 = ln 5.71/0.248 = 7.02. A numerical integration of ∫ dy/(y − y*) gives the same 7.02.
Height of a transfer unit: H<sub>OG</sub> = G/(K<sub>y</sub> a) = 0.015/0.040 = 0.375 m. Unit check: kmol/(m²·s) divided by kmol/(m³·s) is m.
Packed height: Z = H<sub>OG</sub> × N<sub>OG</sub> = 0.375 × 7.02 = 2.63 m. A design would add a margin for maldistribution and round to about 3 m.

Assumptions: dilute gas, so G, L and K<sub>y</sub> a are constant and the (1 − y)<sub>lm</sub> correction is negligible (y ≤ 0.03 changes it by under 2 %); isothermal operation, so m stays at 1.1; both lines straight, which the log mean requires.

Check by stages: the same column holds N = ln[20 × 0.248 + 0.752]/ln 1.33 = 6.11 ideal stages, and HETP = H<sub>OG</sub> ln λ/(λ − 1) with λ = 1/A = 0.752 gives 0.431 m; 6.11 × 0.431 = 2.63 m, the same height.

bank.q: A gas dissolves into a liquid (D<sub>A</sub> = 1.8×10⁻⁹ m²/s, k<sub>L</sub> = 1.0×10⁻⁴ m/s, C<sub>Ai</sub> = 1.0 mol/m³) where it undergoes a first-order reaction. Calculate Ha, E and the flux for k = 2 s⁻¹ and for k = 5000 s⁻¹, decide the regime in each case, and check whether the fast case is limited by the reactant B (C<sub>B</sub> = 500 mol/m³, D<sub>B</sub> = 1.0×10⁻⁹ m²/s, one mole of B per mole of A).
outline: E∞ check for the fast case
answer: Without reaction the flux is N⁰ = k<sub>L</sub>(C<sub>Ai</sub> − 0) = 1.0×10⁻⁴ × 1.0 = 1.0×10⁻⁴ mol/(m²·s), taking the bulk concentration of free A as zero.

answer.text: Hatta number, which compares reaction in the film with diffusion through it:
The two cases:

answer: Slow case: Ha = 0.60 lies between 0.3 and 3, so some reaction happens inside the film and raises the flux by 12 %. Most of the reaction takes place in the bulk liquid. Its main benefit is to keep the bulk concentration of free A low, which protects the driving force down the column.

Fast case: Ha = 30 > 3, so A is used up within a thin layer at the interface, of thickness √(D<sub>A</sub>/k) = √(1.8×10⁻⁹/5000) = 0.60 µm against a film of D<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>L</sub> = 18 µm. The flux is thirty times the physical value and no longer depends on k<sub>L</sub>: N = √(k D<sub>A</sub>) C<sub>Ai</sub>.

Check on B: the instantaneous-reaction limit is E∞ = 1 + D<sub>B</sub> C<sub>B</sub>/(b D<sub>A</sub> C<sub>Ai</sub>) = 1 + (1.0×10⁻⁹ × 500)/(1 × 1.8×10⁻⁹ × 1.0) = 1 + 278 = 279. Since Ha = 30 is far below 279, B is not depleted at the interface and the pseudo-first-order result E ≈ Ha holds.

If C<sub>Ai</sub> rose tenfold (a richer gas), E∞ would fall to 28.8, close to Ha; then B would run short near the interface and the true E would lie below both, so the design must check E∞ at the richest gas condition.
Assumptions: film model; first-order (or pseudo-first-order, B in excess) kinetics; isothermal; the physical k<sub>L</sub> and D<sub>A</sub> are unchanged by reaction; bulk free A negligible.
Check: in the fast regime the penetration theory gives the same E ≈ Ha, so the choice of film model does not change the answer.

bank.q: Compare tray and packed contactors for gas absorption. Discuss stage efficiency, HTU, pressure drop, turndown, liquid rate and fouling, using the duty of a dilute absorber that needs N<sub>OG</sub> = 7.02 with H<sub>OG</sub> = 0.375 m (6.11 ideal stages, λ = 0.752) and sieve trays with E<sub>MV</sub> = 0.70 at 0.6 m spacing.
outline: Height for the stated duty, both ways
answer: Trays make contact in steps: on each tray the gas bubbles through a liquid pool, the phases approach equilibrium and separate. Height follows from ideal stages, tray efficiency and tray spacing. Packing gives continuous contact over a wetted surface; height follows from Z = H<sub>OG</sub> × N<sub>OG</sub>, where H<sub>OG</sub> = G/(K<sub>y</sub> a) carries the packing performance and N<sub>OG</sub> the difficulty of the separation.
Packed height for the duty: Z = 0.375 × 7.02 = 2.63 m of packing (HETP = H<sub>OG</sub> ln λ/(λ − 1) = 0.431 m, and 6.11 × 0.431 = 2.63 m).

Tray height: Lewis's relation gives E<sub>o</sub> = ln[1 + 0.70 × (0.752 − 1)]/ln 0.752 = ln 0.826/ln 0.752 = 0.669. Real trays = 6.11/0.669 = 9.1, so 10 trays; at 0.6 m spacing that is 10 × 0.6 = 6.0 m of tray section, more than twice the packed height.

Pressure drop. Each sieve tray costs the gas the head of its liquid pool plus the dry-plate loss, typically about 0.5 to 1 kPa; ten trays take roughly 5 to 10 kPa. Random packing in absorbers is usually designed for a few hundred pascals per metre, so 2.63 m costs well under 1 kPa. For a large gas flow at near-atmospheric pressure (flue gas, ventilation air) the fan power saved makes packing the clear choice.

answer.text: Other factors:

head: Factor
Trays
Packing
rows: E<sub>MV</sub> per tray; overall E<sub>o</sub> depends on λ
H<sub>OG</sub> from K<sub>y</sub> a; needs good wetting
poor: below the minimum wetting rate, a falls
risk of flooding at lower gas rate
better: trays can be cleaned through manholes
worse: packing plugs and must be removed
ceramic or plastic packing is cheap

answer: Efficiency and λ. A tray absorber with λ < 1 has E<sub>o</sub> below E<sub>MV</sub>, so its tray count rises faster than 1/E<sub>MV</sub> suggests; a packed column's N<sub>OG</sub> rises instead. Both penalties come from the same cause, a small driving force near the dilute end.

Maldistribution. Packed columns lose performance if liquid channels to the wall; tall beds need redistributors every few metres. Trays are less sensitive but suffer from weeping at low gas rates and entrainment at high ones.

Recommendation for this duty: a dilute gas, clean service and no heat removal favour packing: 2.6 m of packing (about 3 m with margin) against 6 m of trays, and a pressure drop around a tenth as large. Trays would win if the liquid carried solids, if the liquid rate were too low to wet the packing, if the column diameter were large, or if heat had to be removed between stages.
Check: both designs treat the same separation, 7.02 transfer units or 6.11 ideal stages; they differ only in how much height and pressure drop each unit of separation costs.

bank.q: Analyse how gas velocity and liquid viscosity affect k<sub>G</sub>, k<sub>L</sub> and the overall resistance in a packed absorber. Use the base case k<sub>y</sub> = 0.050 kmol/(m²·s), k<sub>x</sub> = 0.080 kmol/(m²·s), m = 1.5, and the exponents of Onda's correlations: k<sub>G</sub> ∝ G<sup>0.7</sup> and k<sub>L</sub> ∝ L<sup>2/3</sup> μ<sub>L</sub><sup>−5/6</sup> D<sub>L</sub><sup>1/2</sup>.
outline: Physical reasons: thinner gas film, thicker and slower liquid film
Correlation exponents and diffusivity link to viscosity
Effect on H<sub>OG</sub>; limits from flooding and pressure drop
answer: Gas velocity. A faster gas thins the gas-side boundary layer and adds turbulence, so k<sub>G</sub> (and k<sub>y</sub>) rises. In packed beds the gas-side Sherwood number varies roughly as Re<sub>G</sub><sup>0.7</sup>, which gives k<sub>G</sub> ∝ G<sup>0.7</sup> at fixed packing. Gas velocity hardly touches k<sub>L</sub>. It also raises the pressure drop, roughly with the square of velocity, and brings the column towards flooding.

Liquid viscosity. A more viscous liquid flows as a thicker, slower film with less surface renewal, and its diffusivity falls: the Wilke–Chang and Stokes–Einstein relations give D<sub>L</sub> ∝ T/μ<sub>L</sub>. With Onda's exponents, k<sub>L</sub> ∝ μ<sub>L</sub><sup>−5/6</sup> at fixed D, and with D ∝ 1/μ another factor μ<sub>L</sub><sup>−1/2</sup>, so k<sub>L</sub> ∝ μ<sub>L</sub><sup>−4/3</sup> overall. Viscosity also lowers the wetted area, which this estimate ignores.

answer.text: Base case and the two changes (resistances on the gas basis, m²·s/kmol):

answer: Case A. k<sub>y</sub> rises by 1.5<sup>0.7</sup> = 1.328, the gas resistance falls from 20.0 to 15.06, and K<sub>y</sub> rises by 38.75/33.81 = 1.146, only 15 %, because half the resistance was in the liquid film, which the gas rate does not touch.

The tower height does not fall. H<sub>OG</sub> = G/(K<sub>y</sub> a) rises by 1.5/1.146 = 1.31 at the same a, so each transfer unit needs 31 % more packing. Higher gas velocity buys a smaller diameter, not a shorter tower, and costs pressure drop.

Case B. Doubling μ<sub>L</sub> multiplies k<sub>x</sub> by 2<sup>−4/3</sup> = 0.397, so the liquid term grows from 18.75 to 47.25 and K<sub>y</sub> falls by 42 %. The controlling film shifts: the liquid now carries 70 % of the resistance. Even if D did not change, the flow effect alone (factor 2<sup>−5/6</sup> = 0.561) would cut K<sub>y</sub> by 27 %.

Interpretation through m. The result of each change depends on the shares before it. For a very soluble gas (small m, gas-film controlled) a higher gas rate helps nearly in proportion to G<sup>0.7</sup> and viscosity barely matters; for a sparingly soluble gas (large m) the reverse holds.

Practical responses: for a viscous solvent, heat it (μ falls quickly with temperature) as long as solubility allows, use packing with a large specific area, or choose a reacting solvent so that E multiplies k<sub>L</sub>. To exploit the gas side, raise the gas rate up to about 70 to 80 % of flooding, not beyond.
Check: in case A the new gas share is 15.06/33.81 = 44.5 %, and in case B 20.0/67.25 = 29.7 %, consistent with the table.

bank.q: Evaluate the film, penetration and surface-renewal theories against experimental Sherwood-number correlations. Which is most useful for design, and why? Use the Schmidt-number exponents of the standard correlations and the oxygen data k<sub>L</sub> = 4.0×10⁻⁵ m/s at D = 2.1×10⁻⁹ m²/s.
outline: What each theory predicts and what it leaves to fit
Translate k ∝ D<sup>n</sup> into Sh ∝ Sc<sup>1−n</sup>
answer: All three theories need one fitted parameter (δ, t or s) to give the magnitude of k, so they cannot be judged on magnitude. They differ in how k scales with diffusivity, and that is what experiments test.
At fixed flow, a correlation Sh = C Re<sup>a</sup> Sc<sup>b</sup> means k = C (D/L) Re<sup>a</sup> (ν/D)<sup>b</sup> ∝ D<sup>1−b</sup>. So each theory predicts a Schmidt exponent:

answer.text: Prediction against data:

head: Source
k ∝
Sc exponent b
rows: laminar boundary layer on a solid (flat plate, sphere, Linton–Sherwood pipe)

answer: Reading the table. No correlation has b = 0, so film theory's k ∝ D is contradicted everywhere. At free gas–liquid surfaces (packed-tower liquid films, bubbles) b = 1/2, as penetration and renewal predict. At solid walls b = 1/3, which neither theory gives: the velocity falls to zero at a solid wall, and boundary-layer theory, not surface renewal, describes it.

Second-solute test with the oxygen data. A solute with D = 1.2×10⁻⁹ m²/s in the same vessel is predicted to have k<sub>L</sub> = 4.0×10⁻⁵ × (1.2/2.1) = 2.29×10⁻⁵ m/s by film theory, and 4.0×10⁻⁵ × (1.2/2.1)<sup>1/2</sup> = 3.02×10⁻⁵ m/s by penetration or renewal. A solid-wall boundary layer would give 4.0×10⁻⁵ × (1.2/2.1)<sup>2/3</sup> = 2.75×10⁻⁵ m/s. The spread of 30 % is easily measured, and gas–liquid data side with the √D theories.

Magnitude check of penetration theory: liquid running over packing pieces about 10 mm long at a surface speed near 0.1 m/s has t ≈ 0.1 s, giving k<sub>L</sub> = 2√(2.0×10⁻⁹/(π × 0.1)) = 1.6×10⁻⁴ m/s, the right order for packed towers. The theory gives sensible numbers when t can be estimated from the flow.

answer.text: Strengths and weaknesses for design:

head: Theory
Useful for
Weak at
rows: two-resistance sums; reaction regimes and Ha; quick algebra
wrong D scaling; δ has no physical meaning
bubbles, falling films, short contact; D scaling
s must be fitted; no flow model for it

answer: Enhancement factors for reaction come out nearly the same in all three theories (for example E ≈ Ha in the fast regime), so the simplest, film theory, is used for reaction design without loss.

Verdict: for sizing equipment none of the theories replaces an empirical correlation Sh = f(Re, Sc) for the actual geometry. Penetration and surface renewal are the most useful for scaling a measured k<sub>L</sub> from one solute to another at gas–liquid surfaces, because their √D law matches data. Film theory is the most useful framework for calculation (resistances in series, Hatta number) even though its D dependence is wrong. A design engineer uses a correlation for the number, penetration theory for the scaling, and film theory for the bookkeeping.

bank.q: A gas (G = 0.020 kmol/(m²·s)) carrying 1.0 mol% CO₂ must be cleaned to 0.05 mol% with an amine solution. In plain water m = 1650 at 1 atm and 25 °C. For the packing, k<sub>y</sub> a = 0.10 kmol/(m³·s), physical k<sub>L</sub> a = 0.010 s⁻¹, a = 200 m²/m³ and the liquid holds c = 55 kmol/m³. The pseudo-first-order rate constant is k = 1.5×10⁴ s⁻¹ and D<sub>CO₂</sub> = 1.5×10⁻⁹ m²/s. Choose a tray or packed contactor and size it.
outline: Hatta number, regime and E∞ check
N<sub>OG</sub> with y* ≈ 0, H<sub>OG</sub> and Z
Why stages are a poor measure here
answer: Physical absorption first. The liquid-side coefficient on a mole-fraction basis is k<sub>x</sub> a = k<sub>L</sub> a c = 0.010 × 55 = 0.55 kmol/(m³·s). The liquid resistance on the gas basis is m/(k<sub>x</sub> a) = 1650/0.55 = 3000 m³·s/kmol, against 1/(k<sub>y</sub> a) = 10 for the gas. H<sub>OG</sub> would be 0.020 × 3010 = 60 m, and the solvent would saturate at a liquid mole fraction of only 6×10⁻⁶. Water alone cannot do this duty.

Reaction regime. k<sub>L</sub> = k<sub>L</sub> a/a = 0.010/200 = 5.0×10⁻⁵ m/s. Ha = √(k D)/k<sub>L</sub> = √(1.5×10⁴ × 1.5×10⁻⁹)/5.0×10⁻⁵ = 4.74×10⁻³/5.0×10⁻⁵ = 94.9. With Ha far above 3 the reaction is fast and occurs in the film, so E ≈ Ha.

Check on the amine. At the gas inlet the interface concentration is at most C<sub>Ai</sub> = (y/m) c = (0.010/1650) × 55 kmol/m³ = 3.3×10⁻⁴ kmol/m³ = 0.33 mol/m³. With 2.5 kmol/m³ of amine, two moles per mole of CO₂ and D<sub>B</sub>/D<sub>A</sub> ≈ 0.6, E∞ = 1 + 0.6 × 2500/(2 × 0.33) ≈ 2250, far above 95, so the pseudo-first-order result holds as long as the amine is not heavily loaded.

answer.text: Overall coefficient with reaction:

answer: K<sub>y</sub> a = 1/41.6 = 0.0240 kmol/(m³·s). The liquid film still carries 76 % of the resistance, so a faster amine or more interfacial area would help more than higher gas turbulence.
Transfer units. The fast reaction keeps free CO₂ in the bulk liquid near zero, so y* ≈ 0 throughout and N<sub>OG</sub> = ∫ dy/y = ln(y<sub>1</sub>/y<sub>2</sub>) = ln(0.010/0.0005) = ln 20 = 3.00.
Height: H<sub>OG</sub> = G/(K<sub>y</sub> a) = 0.020/0.0240 = 0.833 m, so Z = 0.833 × 3.00 = 2.50 m. With a 20 % margin for maldistribution and amine loading, specify about 3.0 m of packing.

Stages. With y* ≈ 0 one ideal stage would remove all the CO₂, so the ideal-stage count is meaningless here; a tray would have to be rated by its own rate-based efficiency. The rate-based HTU and NTU method is the right tool for reactive absorption.

Choice: packing. The reaction runs in the film, so the duty depends on interfacial area, which packing supplies at low pressure drop. Amine solutions foam, which packing tolerates better than trays, and plastic or stainless packing resists corrosion. Trays would be preferred only if a slow reaction needed large liquid holdup or if the heat of reaction had to be removed between stages.

Further checks: the solvent must carry at least 2 × 0.020 × (0.010 − 0.0005) = 3.8×10⁻⁴ kmol of amine per m² per second, and the liquid rate must also exceed the minimum wetting rate of the packing; the heat of reaction raises the liquid temperature, which speeds the reaction but lowers solubility; and if the gas film became controlling (say with a much faster amine), Z could not fall below G/(k<sub>y</sub> a) × N<sub>OG</sub> = 0.20 × 3.00 = 0.60 m.

glossary.def: A coefficient that gives mass flux per unit concentration driving force across a fluid phase.
Mass transfer from a moving fluid to a surface or another fluid, helped by bulk flow and turbulence.
Transfer of a component from one phase to another across their interface, as in absorption or extraction.
A coefficient for one phase film, such as gas-film k<sub>y</sub> or liquid-film k<sub>x</sub>.
A coefficient based on the total driving force from bulk gas to bulk liquid, written K<sub>y</sub> or K<sub>x</sub>.
A constant relating gas partial pressure to the liquid composition at equilibrium, p<sub>A</sub> = H x<sub>A</sub>; divided by the total pressure it gives the slope m of y* = m x.
A plot of equilibrium vapor composition against liquid composition at fixed temperature and pressure.
A material-balance line relating vapor and liquid compositions in a stage or packed contactor.
A model with one gas film and one liquid film in series, with equilibrium at the interface.
A model that treats resistance as a stagnant film of fixed thickness δ, giving k<sub>c</sub> = D/δ.
A model in which fluid elements stay at the interface for a fixed exposure time t, giving k<sub>c</sub> = 2√(D/(πt)).
A model in which surface elements are replaced at a renewal rate s, giving k<sub>c</sub> = √(Ds).
Turbulent mixing that increases transport beyond molecular diffusion, described by eddy diffusivity.
A dimensionless mass transfer coefficient, Sh = k<sub>c</sub> L/D<sub>AB</sub>.
A dimensionless ratio of momentum diffusivity to mass diffusivity, Sc = μ/(ρD<sub>AB</sub>).
A dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces, Re = ρuL/μ, used in flow correlations.
An analogy linking mass transfer and friction through j<sub>D</sub> = (k<sub>c</sub>/u)Sc<sup>2/3</sup> = f/2.
A hypothetical stage that leaves its exiting vapor and liquid in equilibrium.
The ratio of the composition change in a real stage to that in an ideal equilibrium stage.
The packed height needed for one transfer unit, H<sub>OG</sub> = G/(K<sub>y</sub> a).
A dimensionless measure of separation duty, N<sub>OG</sub> = ∫ dy/(y − y*).
A continuous-contact column filled with packing that provides interfacial area for mass transfer.
A stagewise column with plates or trays on which vapor bubbles through liquid.
The factor by which a chemical reaction increases mass flux above physical absorption.
A dimensionless number comparing reaction rate to diffusion rate in the liquid film.
Gas absorption in which the dissolved gas reacts with a component in the liquid.
